title: Rhetoric and style: figures of speech and making a speech
intro: Persians have studied the art of speaking well for a thousand years, and the figures their scholars named – simile, metaphor, indirect expression, exaggeration, antithesis, rhymed prose, wordplay, allusion – are not museum pieces: you will hear every one of them at a family dinner. This lesson names the nine main figures with classical and everyday examples, then shows how Iranians give a short speech or a toast at a wedding or a farewell, ending with a model wedding speech.
goals: recognise and name تشبیه، استعاره، کنایه، مبالغه، تضاد، تکرار، سجع، جناس and تلمیح in poetry, prose and conversation
explain how a classical line by Saadi, Ferdowsi, Rumi or Hafez works
use everyday figures of speech naturally and understand them when you hear them
give a short speech or toast at a wedding or farewell with the right formulas

sections.title: Speaking well, an old art
sections.intro: An essay on Persian rhetoric (بلاغت). Notice that the essay itself uses the devices it describes – an example, a quotation, a contrast – and that Arabic technical terms (تشبیه، استعاره، سجع…) sit inside very Persian sentences.

sentences.fa: در سنت ادبی فارسی، سخن گفتن تنها وسیله‌ی رساندن پیام نیست، بلکه هنری است که آموختنی است.
sentences.r: dar sonnat-e adabi-ye fārsi, sokhan goftan tanhā vasile-ye resāndan-e payām nist, balke honar-i ast ke āmukhtani ast.
sentences.en: In the Persian literary tradition, speaking is not merely a way of conveying a message but an art that can be learned.

sentences.fa: دانشمندان قدیم این هنر را «بلاغت» می‌نامیدند و آن را در سه دانش «معانی»، «بیان» و «بدیع» بررسی می‌کردند.
sentences.r: dāneshmandān-e ghadim in honar rā «balāghat» mi-nāmidand va ān rā dar se dānesh-e «ma'āni», «bayān» o «badi'» barrasi mi-kardand.
sentences.en: Scholars of old called this art balāghat (eloquence) and studied it in three sciences: ma'āni, bayān and badi'.

sentences.fa: «بیان» از شیوه‌های گوناگون گفتن یک معنا سخن می‌گوید: تشبیه، استعاره، مجاز و کنایه.
sentences.r: «bayān» az shive-hā-ye gunāgun-e goftan-e yek ma'nā sokhan mi-guyad: tashbih, este'āre, majāz o kenāye.
sentences.en: Bayān deals with the different ways of saying one and the same thing: simile, metaphor, figurative usage and indirect expression.

sentences.fa: «بدیع» به زیبایی‌های لفظی و معنوی کلام می‌پردازد، مانند سجع، جناس، تضاد و تلمیح.
sentences.r: «badi'» be zibāyi-hā-ye lafzi va ma'navi-ye kalām mi-pardāzad, mānand-e saj', jenās, tazādd o talmih.
sentences.en: Badi' deals with the beauties of sound and sense in speech, such as rhymed prose, wordplay, antithesis and allusion.

sentences.fa: ساده‌ترین این شگردها تشبیه است: «چهره‌اش مثل ماه است.»
sentences.r: sāde-tarin-e in shegerd-hā tashbih ast: «chehre-ash mesl-e māh ast.»
sentences.en: The simplest of these devices is the simile: 'Her face is like the moon.'

sentences.fa: در استعاره، یکی از دو سوی تشبیه حذف می‌شود و شاعر به جای «یار»، تنها از «سرو» یا «ماه» سخن می‌گوید.
sentences.r: dar este'āre, yek-i az do su-ye tashbih hazf mi-shavad va shā'er be jā-ye «yār», tanhā az «sarv» yā «māh» sokhan mi-guyad.
sentences.en: In a metaphor one of the two sides of the comparison is dropped, and instead of 'the beloved' the poet speaks only of 'the cypress' or 'the moon'.

sentences.fa: کنایه معنایی پنهان را از راهی غیرمستقیم می‌رساند؛ «در خانه‌اش همیشه باز است» یعنی او مهمان‌نواز است.
sentences.r: kenāye ma'nā-yi penhān rā az rāh-i gheyr-e-mostaghim mi-resānad; «dar-e khāne-ash hamishe bāz ast» ya'ni u mehmān-navāz ast.
sentences.en: Kenāye conveys a hidden meaning indirectly: 'his door is always open' means that he is hospitable.

sentences.fa: سعدی در گلستان با سجع، نثر را به موسیقی نزدیک کرده است.
sentences.r: Sa'di dar Golestān bā saj', nasr rā be musighi nazdik karde ast.
sentences.en: In the Golestan, Saadi uses rhymed prose to bring prose close to music.

sentences.fa: این شگردها تنها به کتاب‌ها محدود نیستند و در گفت‌وگوی روزانه‌ی ایرانیان نیز فراوان به کار می‌روند.
sentences.r: in shegerd-hā tanhā be ketāb-hā mahdud nistand va dar goft-o-gu-ye ruzāne-ye Irāniyān niz farāvān be kār mi-ravand.
sentences.en: These devices are not confined to books; Iranians use them constantly in everyday conversation too.

sentences.fa: مردم به جای «خیلی خسته‌ام» می‌گویند «از پا افتادم» و به جای «خیلی خندیدیم» می‌گویند «از خنده مردیم».
sentences.r: mardom be jā-ye «kheyli khaste-am» mi-guyand «az pā oftādam» va be jā-ye «kheyli khandidim» mi-guyand «az khande mordim».
sentences.en: Instead of 'I'm very tired' people say 'I've fallen off my feet', and instead of 'we laughed a lot' they say 'we died laughing'.

sentences.fa: این مبالغه‌ها کسی را فریب نمی‌دهند، بلکه به سخن گرمی و رنگ می‌بخشند.
sentences.r: in mobālaghe-hā kas-i rā farib nemi-dahand, balke be sokhan garmi o rang mi-bakhshand.
sentences.en: These exaggerations deceive no one; they give warmth and colour to speech.

sentences.fa: هنر سخن در مراسم رسمی، از عروسی تا بدرقه‌ی همکاران، اهمیتی ویژه دارد.
sentences.r: honar-e sokhan dar marāsem-e rasmi, az arusi tā badraghe-ye hamkārān, ahammiyat-i vizhe dārad.
sentences.en: The art of speaking matters particularly at formal occasions, from weddings to farewells for colleagues.

sentences.fa: سخنران خوب سخن خود را با سپاس و خوشامدگویی آغاز می‌کند و با آرزوی خیر به پایان می‌برد.
sentences.r: sokhanrān-e khub sokhan-e khod rā bā sepās o khoshāmad-guyi āghāz mi-konad va bā ārezu-ye kheyr be pāyān mi-barad.
sentences.en: A good speaker begins with thanks and a welcome and ends with good wishes.

sentences.fa: او شعری کوتاه از حافظ یا سعدی می‌خواند تا سخنش را دلنشین‌تر کند.
sentences.r: u she'r-i kutāh az Hāfez yā Sa'di mi-khānad tā sokhan-ash rā delneshin-tar konad.
sentences.en: He or she recites a short poem by Hafez or Saadi to make the speech more moving.

sentences.fa: با این همه، زیاده‌روی در آرایه‌ها سخن را از صداقت تهی می‌کند.
sentences.r: bā in hame, ziyāde-ravi dar ārāye-hā sokhan rā az sedāghat tohi mi-konad.
sentences.en: Even so, overdoing the ornaments empties a speech of sincerity.

sentences.fa: شیوه‌ی سعدی را «سهل و ممتنع» خوانده‌اند: سخنی که ساده به نظر می‌رسد، اما تقلید آن ناممکن است.
sentences.r: shive-ye Sa'di rā «sahl o momtane'» khānde-and: sokhan-i ke sāde be nazar mi-resad, ammā taghlid-e ān nā-momken ast.
sentences.en: Saadi's style has been called 'easy and impossible': speech that looks simple but cannot be imitated.

questions.q: Which branch of rhetoric deals with simile, metaphor and indirect expression?

options: A metaphor drops one side of the comparison
A simile is only used in poetry

questions.q: «از خنده مردیم» is an example of…

It is full of Arabic words

sections.title: Nine figures, one tradition
sections.md:
Classical Persian rhetoric was built on Arabic models, so its terms are Arabic: [[تشبیه|tashbih|simile]], [[استعاره|este'āre|metaphor]], [[کنایه|kenāye|indirect expression]], [[مبالغه|mobālaghe|exaggeration]], [[تضاد|tazādd|antithesis]], [[تکرار|tekrār|repetition]], [[سجع|saj'|rhymed prose]], [[جناس|jenās|wordplay]], [[تلمیح|talmih|allusion]]. Iranian schoolchildren learn them all in literature classes, and the modern Persian umbrella word for them is [[آرایه‌های ادبی|ārāye-hā-ye adabi|literary ornaments]].

Two things make them worth learning even if you never write a poem:

- **They are everywhere in speech.** A Tehrani who says [[سرم شلوغ است|sar-am sholugh ast|my head is crowded]] (I'm busy) is using kenāye; a mother who says [[صد بار گفتم!|sad bār goftam!|I've said it a hundred times!]] is using mobālaghe.
- **They are the grammar of a good speech.** Weddings, farewells, memorial gatherings, birthdays and staff parties all call for a few words – and Iranians expect those words to be shaped: a contrast, an image, a line of Hafez, a wish.

The first two language sections below take the figures in two families – comparison and indirection, then sound and sense. The third gives you the building blocks of a speech.

items.en: point of comparison (what two things share)

ex.en: There was a dig in what he said.

items.en: allusion (to a story, verse or event)

ex.en: I'd like to say a few words.

sections.title: Comparison and indirection: تشبیه، استعاره، کنایه
sections.md:
**تشبیه (simile)** has four parts, and Persian school grammars name them all: the thing compared ([[مشبه|moshabbah]]), what it is compared to ([[مشبه‌به|moshabbah-on-beh]]), the comparison word ([[ادات تشبیه|adāt-e tashbih]]: مثل، مانند، چون، همچون) and the shared quality ([[وجه شبه|vajh-e shabah]]). In *her face is like the moon in its brightness* all four are present. Drop the comparison word and the quality and you get the strong, compact simile that Persian poets love: [[قد سرو|ghadd-e sarv|a cypress stature]].

**استعاره (metaphor)** goes one step further: only the image remains. In classical poetry the images are a fixed code – [[سرو|sarv|cypress]] = the beloved's tall figure, [[نرگس|narges|narcissus]] = the eye, [[لعل|la'l|ruby]] = the lips, [[ماه|māh|moon]] = the face or the beloved. Everyday Persian keeps the code: [[ماه من|māh-e man|my moon]] is still *my darling*.

**کنایه (indirect expression)** says one thing and means another that follows from it: an open door means hospitality, a crowded head means being busy. Most Persian idioms are kenāye, and many have a moral sting.

examples.fa: بنی‌آدم اعضای یکدیگرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند
examples.r: bani-ādam a'zā-ye yekdigar-and / ke dar āfarinesh ze yek gowhar-and
examples.en: The children of Adam are limbs of one another, / for in creation they are of one essence.
examples.note: Saadi, Golestan. A تشبیه بلیغ: people are limbs, with no 'like'. The image is carried through the poem: when one limb hurts, the others cannot rest.

examples.fa: چهره‌اش مثل ماه است.
examples.r: chehre-ash mesl-e māh ast.
examples.en: Her face is like the moon.
examples.note: مشبه چهره، مشبه‌به ماه، ادات مثل; the shared quality (beauty, radiance) is left to the listener.

examples.fa: ماه من، کجایی؟
examples.r: māh-e man, kojā-yi?
examples.en: Where are you, my darling?
examples.note: استعاره: the person has disappeared behind the image.

examples.fa: سرش خیلی شلوغ است.
examples.r: sar-ash kheyli sholugh ast.
examples.en: He's very busy.

examples.fa: نمک خورد و نمکدان شکست.
examples.r: namak khord o namakdān shekast.
examples.en: He bit the hand that fed him.
examples.lit: he ate the salt and broke the salt-cellar
examples.note: Sharing salt (bread and salt) is the old sign of hospitality and trust.

examples.fa: پدربزرگم خیلی دست و دلباز بود.
examples.r: pedarbozorg-am kheyli dast o delbāz bud.
examples.en: My grandfather was very generous.
examples.lit: very open of hand and heart

examples.fa: از پا افتادم.
examples.r: az pā oftādam.
examples.en: I'm exhausted.
examples.note: Kenāye and mild exaggeration together – the normal state of conversational Persian.

sections.title: Sound and sense: مبالغه، تضاد، تکرار، سجع، جناس، تلمیح
sections.md:
The second family plays with **sound** (rhyme, echo, repetition) and with **sense** (opposites, impossibilities, references to stories everyone knows).

- **مبالغه** stretches a claim beyond belief – and nobody objects.
- **تضاد** puts opposites side by side: old and young, night and day, laughter and tears.
- **تکرار** repeats for emphasis or music. In the ghazal it is built into the form as the [[ردیف|radif]], the refrain that follows every rhyme.
- **سجع** is rhyme in prose: two clauses end in words that chime. Saadi's Golestan is the model.
- **جناس** pairs words that look or sound alike but mean different things – from exact homonyms to words that differ in one letter.
- **تلمیح** alludes to a story, a verse or a person the listener knows: Joseph and Jacob, Leyli and Majnun, Rostam.

examples.fa: اگر آن ترک شیرازی به دست آرد دل ما را / به خال هندویش بخشم سمرقند و بخارا را
examples.r: agar ān tork-e Shirāzi be dast ārad del-e mā rā / be khāl-e hendu-yash bakhsham Samarghand o Bokhārā rā
examples.en: If that Turk of Shiraz would take my heart in her hand, / for her dark mole I would give away Samarkand and Bukhara.
examples.note: Hafez. مبالغه: two great cities for a beauty spot. ترک (a fair-skinned beauty) and هندو (dark) also make a تضاد.

examples.fa: توانا بود هر که دانا بود / ز دانش دل پیر برنا بود
examples.r: tavānā bovad har ke dānā bovad / ze dānesh del-e pir bornā bovad
examples.en: Powerful is he who is wise; / through knowledge an old heart is young.
examples.note: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh. تضاد between پیر 'old' and برنا 'young'; توانا and دانا chime.

examples.fa: یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان غم مخور / کلبه‌ی احزان شود روزی گلستان غم مخور
examples.r: Yusof-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be Kan'ān gham makhor / kolbe-ye ahzān shavad ruzi golestān gham makhor
examples.en: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan – do not grieve; / the house of sorrows will one day be a rose garden – do not grieve.
examples.note: Hafez. تلمیح to Joseph and his grieving father Jacob; تکرار in the refrain غم مخور; تضاد between کلبه‌ی احزان and گلستان.

examples.fa: بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها حکایت می‌کند
examples.r: beshnow in ney chon shekāyat mi-konad / az jodāyi-hā hekāyat mi-konad
examples.en: Listen to this reed, how it complains, / telling the tale of separations.
examples.note: Rumi, the opening of the Masnavi. جناس: شکایت and حکایت differ in one letter. Many editions print «بشنو از نی».

examples.fa: منت خدای را عز و جل که طاعتش موجب قربت است و به شکر اندرش مزید نعمت.
examples.r: mennat khodāy rā 'azza va jall ke tā'at-ash mujeb-e ghorbat ast va be shokr andar-ash mazid-e ne'mat.
examples.en: Praise be to God, mighty and glorious, obedience to whom brings one near Him, and in thanking whom lies an increase of blessing.
examples.note: Saadi, the first sentence of the Golestan. سجع: قربت / نعمت. The second verb (است) is left out of the second clause.

examples.fa: هر نفسی که فرو می‌رود ممد حیات است و چون برمی‌آید مفرح ذات.
examples.r: har nafasi ke foru mi-ravad momedd-e hayāt ast va chon bar-mi-āyad mofarreh-e zāt.
examples.en: Every breath that goes in sustains life, and every breath that comes out gladdens the soul.
examples.note: سجع: حیات / ذات; تضاد: فرو رفتن 'go down' / برآمدن 'come up'.

examples.fa: آرام آرام، قدم به قدم، به هدف نزدیک شدیم.
examples.r: ārām ārām, ghadam be ghadam, be hadaf nazdik shodim.
examples.en: Slowly, step by step, we got close to our goal.
examples.note: Everyday تکرار: doubling makes Persian adverbs gentler or more vivid.

sections.title: The shape of a short speech
sections.md:
Whether it is a wedding, a colleague's retirement or a friend leaving for abroad, an Iranian speech of a few minutes tends to follow the same path: **address → permission and modesty → thanks → a story or praise → an image or a line of poetry → a wish → (a toast) → a humble close**. The formulas below are formal but warm; use the shomā forms throughout, even to people you know well, because you are speaking in public.

Two cultural notes. First, modesty is expected: [[من اهل سخنرانی نیستم|man ahl-e sokhanrāni nistam|I'm no speech-maker]] is said even by professional speakers. Second, [[عرض کردن|arz kardan]] is the humble verb for your own words, and [[فرمودن|farmudan]] the honorific verb for other people's: [[همان‌طور که آقای کریمی فرمودند|hamān-towr ke āghā-ye Karimi farmudand|as Mr Karimi said]].

sections.title: A model speech: Reza's toast at Sara and Amir's wedding
sections.intro: Reza, Amir's oldest friend, gives a short speech at the wedding reception. It is spoken, but in the careful register of a public occasion. Each note names the step or the figure of speech.

sentences.fa: مهمانان عزیز، خانواده‌های محترم، سلام عرض می‌کنم.
sentences.r: mehmānān-e aziz, khānevāde-hā-ye mohtaram, salām arz mi-konam.
sentences.en: Dear guests, honoured families, good evening.
sentences.note: Address: guests first, then the two families.

sentences.fa: با اجازه‌ی بزرگترها، چند کلمه‌ای درباره‌ی دوستانم سارا و امیر عرض می‌کنم.
sentences.r: bā ejāze-ye bozorg-tar-hā, chand kalame-i darbāre-ye dustān-am Sārā va Amir arz mi-konam.
sentences.en: With the elders' permission, I'd like to say a few words about my friends Sara and Amir.
sentences.note: Permission – a nod to the older generation – and the humble verb عرض کردن.

sentences.fa: راستش من اهل سخنرانی نیستم، پس قول می‌دهم کوتاه حرف بزنم.
sentences.r: rāst-ash man ahl-e sokhanrāni nistam, pas ghowl mi-daham kutāh harf bezanam.
sentences.en: To be honest I'm no speech-maker, so I promise to keep it short.

sentences.fa: ده سال پیش، امیر را در کلاس زبان دانشگاه شناختم.
sentences.r: dah sāl pish, Amir rā dar kelās-e zabān-e dāneshgāh shenākhtam.
sentences.en: Ten years ago I got to know Amir in a language class at university.

sentences.fa: او آن روزها می‌گفت: «من هرگز ازدواج نمی‌کنم؛ من با کتاب‌هایم ازدواج کرده‌ام!»
sentences.r: u ān ruz-hā mi-goft: «man hargez ezdevāj nemi-konam; man bā ketāb-hā-yam ezdevāj karde-am!»
sentences.en: In those days he used to say, 'I'll never marry – I'm married to my books!'
sentences.note: Gentle humour at the groom's expense – expected, but never at the bride's.

sentences.fa: اما یک روز سارا وارد کتابخانه شد و کتاب‌ها از دست امیر افتاد.
sentences.r: ammā yek ruz Sārā vāred-e ketābkhāne shod va ketāb-hā az dast-e Amir oftād.
sentences.en: But one day Sara walked into the library, and the books fell out of Amir's hands.
sentences.note: Kenāye: the falling books say what nobody needs to spell out.

sentences.fa: از آن روز، امیر دیگر نه درس می‌خواند و نه خواب داشت.
sentences.r: az ān ruz, Amir digar na dars mi-khānd va na khāb dāsht.
sentences.en: From that day on Amir could neither study nor sleep.
sentences.note: مبالغه, and the balanced نه … نه … .

sentences.fa: سارا برای او مثل ماه بود: دور، روشن و زیبا.
sentences.r: Sārā barā-ye u mesl-e māh bud: dur, roshan o zibā.
sentences.en: To him Sara was like the moon: far away, bright and beautiful.
sentences.note: تشبیه with the shared qualities spelled out.

sentences.fa: امروز آن ماه به خانه‌ی امیر آمده است.
sentences.r: emruz ān māh be khāne-ye Amir āmade ast.
sentences.en: Today that moon has come to Amir's house.
sentences.note: The simile becomes a metaphor (استعاره): Sara is now simply 'the moon'.

sentences.fa: سعدی می‌گوید: «بنی‌آدم اعضای یکدیگرند»؛ و امروز این دو نفر به راستی عضو یک خانواده شده‌اند.
sentences.r: Sa'di mi-guyad: «bani-ādam a'zā-ye yekdigar-and»; va emruz in do nafar be rāsti ozv-e yek khānevāde shode-and.
sentences.en: Saadi says, 'The children of Adam are limbs of one another' – and today these two have truly become limbs of one family.
sentences.note: تلمیح and quotation, with a play on اعضا / عضو.

sentences.fa: در زندگی روزهای شاد و روزهای سخت، هر دو، خواهد آمد.
sentences.r: dar zendegi ruz-hā-ye shād va ruz-hā-ye sakht, har do, khāhad āmad.
sentences.en: Life will bring both happy days and hard ones.

sentences.fa: آرزو می‌کنم که در روزهای شاد با هم بخندید و در روزهای سخت دست یکدیگر را بگیرید.
sentences.r: ārezu mi-konam ke dar ruz-hā-ye shād bā ham bekhandid va dar ruz-hā-ye sakht dast-e yekdigar rā begirid.
sentences.en: I wish you laughter together on the happy days, and on the hard days, each other's hand to hold.
sentences.note: The wish, built on تکرار and parallel clauses.

sentences.fa: از پدر و مادر عروس و داماد هم برای این جشن زیبا سپاسگزارم.
sentences.r: az pedar o mādar-e arus o dāmād ham barā-ye in jashn-e zibā sepāsgozār-am.
sentences.en: I'd also like to thank the parents of the bride and groom for this lovely celebration.

sentences.fa: حالا لطفاً همه جام‌هایتان را بالا ببرید.
sentences.r: hālā lotfan hame jām-hā-yetān rā bālā bebarid.
sentences.en: Now would you all please raise your glasses.
sentences.note: The toast – here with sharbat or juice.

sentences.fa: به سلامتی سارا و امیر! به پای هم پیر شوید!
sentences.r: be salāmati-ye Sārā va Amir! be pā-ye ham pir shavid!
sentences.en: To Sara and Amir! May you grow old together!

sentences.fa: زیاده عرضی نیست.
sentences.r: ziyāde arz-i nist.
sentences.en: That's all from me.

questions.q: Which figure is «امروز آن ماه به خانه‌ی امیر آمده است»?
Why does Reza mention the books falling from Amir's hands?
options: To show indirectly that he fell for Sara at first sight
Because Sara worked in the library

questions.q: Which formula does Reza use to close the speech?

sections.title: Speeches, toasts and the bride who went to pick flowers
sections.md:
At an Iranian wedding the most quoted words are not in a speech at all. During the ceremony ([[عقد|aghd]]), seated before the decorated *sofreh*, the bride is asked three times whether she consents. The first two times the guests call out [[عروس رفته گل بچیند!|arus rafte gol bechinad!|the bride has gone to pick flowers!]] – and only the third time does she answer [[بله|bale|yes]], to applause and ululation. It is a ritual of modesty, and a small piece of rhetoric in itself: a pause made meaningful.

Speeches come later, at the reception, and are usually short. A relative or an old friend of the couple speaks, often with a few lines of Hafez or Saadi. Many Iranian celebrations are alcohol-free, so the glasses raised for [[به سلامتی|be salāmati]] may hold sharbat, juice or tea – the toast is about the words, not the drink.

Farewells ([[مهمانی خداحافظی|mehmāni-ye khodāhāfezi|a goodbye party]]) have their own style. Colleagues bring flowers and a box of pastries, someone says [[جایتان خالی خواهد بود|jā-yetān khāli khāhad bud]], and the person leaving answers with thanks and a ritual apology for any trouble they caused: [[اگر بدی دیدید، حلال کنید|agar bad-i didid, halāl konid|if I ever wronged you, forgive me]]. For a friend going abroad, a classic touch is to hold a copy of the Quran or a mirror over the doorway and to pour a bowl of water after the traveller – so that they come back as smoothly as water flows.

sections.title: Tips
items: To tell تشبیه from استعاره, ask: are both things named? «چشمانش مثل نرگس است» is a simile; «نرگس مستش» (her drunken narcissus) is a metaphor.
Kenāye is the hardest figure for learners because it looks literal. If «دستش کج است» (his hand is crooked) seems to make no sense, it is kenāye: he steals.
When you give a speech, write it in the formal register but read it slowly and warmly. Speak the poem, don't rush it – people will often say the second half with you.
One line of poetry is perfect; three is a lecture. Choose a line everyone knows: Saadi's بنی‌آدم, Hafez's یوسف گم‌گشته or a line from the Shahnameh.
Use عرض کردن for your own words and فرمودن for other people's. Mixing them up is a classic learner's slip that Iranians will find charming – but notice.
Everyday mobālaghe is not lying. «یک دنیا ممنون» (a world of thanks) and «صد بار» (a hundred times) are just the normal volume of Persian feeling.

items.fa: با اجازه‌ی ___، چند کلمه‌ای عرض می‌کنم.
items.r: bā ejāze-ye ___, chand kalame-i arz mi-konam.
items.en: With the elders' permission, I'll say a few words.
That's all I have to say.
Her face is like the moon.
Dear guests, I'd like to say a few words.
items.fa: مهمانان عزیز، چند کلمه‌ای عرض می‌کنم.
items.r: mehmānān-e aziz, chand kalame-i arz mi-konam.

items.en: I'm very busy these days. (use a figure of speech)
items.fa: این روزها سرم خیلی شلوغ است.
items.r: in ruz-hā sar-am kheyli sholugh ast.

items.en: We will miss you very much, Mr Karimi.
items.fa: آقای کریمی، جای شما خیلی خالی خواهد بود.
items.r: āghā-ye Karimi, jā-ye shomā kheyli khāli khāhad bud.

items.en: To Sara and Amir! May you grow old together!
items.fa: به سلامتی سارا و امیر! به پای هم پیر شوید!
items.r: be salāmati-ye Sārā va Amir! be pā-ye ham pir shavid!

items.en: I've told you a hundred times!

items.q: [[توانا بود هر که دانا بود / ز دانش دل پیر برنا بود|tavānā bovad har ke dānā bovad / ze dānesh del-e pir bornā bovad]] – which figure links پیر and برنا?
items.explain: پیر 'old' and برنا 'young' are opposites side by side.

items.q: [[شکایت|shekāyat]] and [[حکایت|hekāyat]] in Rumi's first line are an example of…
items.explain: Two words that differ by one letter and mean different things: wordplay (جناس).

items.q: The best English for [[دستش کج است.|dast-ash kaj ast.]]
items.explain: A kenāye: the 'crooked hand' takes what isn't its own.

items.q: [[یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان|Yusof-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be Kan'ān]] uses the story of Joseph. This is…
items.explain: An allusion (تلمیح) to a story every listener knows.

items.q: The best English for [[نمک خورد و نمکدان شکست.|namak khord o namakdān shekast.]]
options: He bit the hand that fed him.
He broke a dish at dinner.
items.explain: Eating someone's salt means accepting their hospitality; breaking the salt-cellar is betrayal.

items.q: Which is a metaphor (استعاره), not a simile?
items.explain: Only the image (ماه) is named; the person it stands for has disappeared.

items.fa: با اجازه‌ی بزرگترها چند کلمه‌ای عرض می‌کنم.
items.r: bā ejāze-ye bozorg-tar-hā chand kalame-i arz mi-konam.
items.en: With the elders' permission I'd like to say a few words.

items.fa: من اهل سخنرانی نیستم، پس سخن را کوتاه می‌کنم.
items.r: man ahl-e sokhanrāni nistam, pas sokhan rā kutāh mi-konam.
items.en: I'm no speech-maker, so I'll keep it short.

items.fa: سارا برای او مثل ماه بود.
items.r: Sārā barā-ye u mesl-e māh bud.
items.en: To him Sara was like the moon.

items.fa: از همه‌ی شما که تشریف آوردید سپاسگزارم.
items.r: az hame-ye shomā ke tashrif āvardid sepāsgozār-am.

items.en: say one thing, mean what it implies

items.fa: آقای کریمی، جای شما خالی خواهد بود.
items.r: āghā-ye Karimi, jā-ye shomā khāli khāhad bud.
items.en: Mr Karimi, we will miss you.
options: Mr Karimi, your seat is free.
Mr Karimi, we will miss you.
My head is full of ideas.
